body: {"total":8,"records":[{"title":"Extended opening hours in community pharmacies and out-of-hours general practice contacts: a regional before-after evaluation with a comparison region","authors":"Brathwaite-Okoro L, Nilsson-Achebe D, Farouk-Hemming S","year":2019,"venue":"Silverbeck Pharmacy Services Research","doi":"10.5555/jpsr.2019.0144","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In one region, 34 community pharmacies extended their opening to 22:00 on weekdays and opened on Sundays for 18 months; a neighbouring region served as comparison. Out-of-hours GP contacts for minor ailments fell by 6 percent relative to the comparison region, and emergency supplies of medicines through the out-of-hours GP service fell by 11 percent. From the payer's perspective, the extended-hours supplement cost 1.8 million a year and valued offsets were 1.4 million, a net annual budget impact of an extra 0.4 million. Emergency department attendances for minor conditions did not change clearly. Pharmacy staffing costs above the supplement were not included."},{"title":"Budget impact of late-night community pharmacy opening: a decision model for an urban health board","authors":"Ilunga-Pearson T, Marchetti-Okafor J","year":2021,"venue":"Pellmoor Health Economics in Practice","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We built a three-year budget impact model of late-night opening for 25 pharmacies serving 600,000 people, from the health board's perspective. Inputs came from pharmacy consultation logs, published unit costs and expert opinion. The base case gave a net cost of 1.2 million over three years. Results were most sensitive to the share of late-night pharmacy consultations that would otherwise have led to an emergency department attendance, which experts placed between 5 and 25 percent; at 25 percent the scheme saved money. The authors call for empirical data on what users would have done without the pharmacy."},{"title":"Sunday opening of community pharmacies and emergency department attendances for minor conditions: an interrupted time series","authors":"Duval-Asante R, Kowalski-Obi M","year":2023,"venue":"Emergency Care Utilisation Studies","doi":"10.5555/ecus.2023.0271","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We analysed weekly emergency department attendances for minor conditions in four towns for two years before and one year after local pharmacies began opening on Sundays. There was no clear change in level or trend of Sunday attendances for minor conditions (level change minus 2 percent, 95 percent CI minus 9 to 6). Attendances for minor conditions on Monday mornings also did not change. The analysis did not include costs. The authors note that Sunday opening was advertised only in pharmacies and that awareness among residents was probably low during the first year."},{"title":"Who uses community pharmacies after 20:00? Late-evening consultations in two cities","authors":"Haldane-Mwangi C, Soto-Brennan K","year":2017,"venue":"Silverbeck Pharmacy Services Research","doi":"10.5555/jpsr.2017.0058","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Pharmacists in 18 late-opening pharmacies in two cities logged 1,850 consultations between 20:00 and closing over four weeks. Emergency supply of a regular medicine made up 38 percent of consultations and minor ailments 27 percent. Users were younger than daytime users and more often shift workers, and 22 percent of users had no registered GP. Pharmacists judged that 31 percent of users would otherwise have contacted the out-of-hours GP service and 9 percent an emergency department, but users were not asked directly. Consultations peaked between 20:00 and 21:00 and were few after 21:30."},{"title":"Pharmacists' experience of working extended hours: staffing, lone working and safety","authors":"Rowntree-Adeyemi F, Petrov-Lindqvist A","year":2022,"venue":"Community Pharmacy Workforce Journal","doi":"10.5555/cpwj.2022.0119","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We conducted in-depth conversations with 24 pharmacists and 9 pharmacy owners in regions that had funded extended opening. Pharmacists described lone working late at night, fear of aggression and theft, and fatigue after long shifts. Owners reported difficulty recruiting pharmacists for evenings and relied on locums, which raised costs above the supplement. Four of the nine owners had reduced their hours within a year. Pharmacists valued being able to help people who had nowhere else to go, but several said the late hours were quiet after 21:00. Participants suggested shared rotas between neighbouring pharmacies and security measures as conditions for continuing."},{"title":"Commissioners' views on paying for extended pharmacy access: a thematic analysis of board papers and discussions","authors":"Achterberg-Nkosi P, Lamont-Iwu R","year":2020,"venue":"Health Policy and Commissioning Review","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We analysed board papers from eleven health authorities that considered extended pharmacy opening between 2014 and 2019 and held discussions with 16 commissioners. Commissioners valued convenience and visible access but doubted claims of savings, because avoided contacts were estimated by pharmacists rather than observed. Several worried that demand moved from daytime services rather than falling. Decisions were often made on the strength of advocacy from pharmacy bodies. Commissioners asked for evidence separated by who uses late opening and for costs that included staffing above the supplement."},{"title":"Combining budget impact estimates from different payers: a methodological review of 42 syntheses","authors":"Gallardo-Whitmore E, Tanaka-Osei B, Lindberg-Ruiz H","year":2024,"venue":"Methods in Health Economic Evidence","doi":"10.5555/mhee.2024.0036","providerType":"review","abstract":"We reviewed 42 evidence syntheses that combined budget impact analyses. Studies differed in perspective, price year, currency, time horizon and the services counted as offsets, and fewer than half reported all five. Pooling budget impact figures across health systems produced estimates that could not be interpreted for any single payer. We recommend structured tables that re-express each estimate in a common price year and currency, report perspective and offsets explicitly, and avoid a pooled figure unless the studies share perspective and setting. Where local decisions are needed, estimates should be re-priced with local unit costs."},{"title":"Public views of late-night pharmacy services: a citizens' panel report","authors":"Regional Citizens' Health Panel","year":2018,"venue":"Citizens' panel report series","providerType":"report","abstract":"A panel of 48 residents discussed late-night pharmacy services over two sessions. Participants valued being able to get medicines and advice after work, especially people working shifts and parents of young children. People without a car said a late pharmacy was only useful if it was on a bus route that ran after 21:00. Some worried about waiting alone late at night and about privacy at the counter. Participants were unsure whether they would have gone to the emergency department instead. The panel recommended publicising late opening and placing late pharmacies near public transport and health centres."}]}
